module_title: Secure and Resilient Architectures — Encryption and Key Management
review_basis: Original SAP Module 03 16:9 WebP visuals 01–08 individually inspected and narration follows exact depicted examples, technical labels and caveats.
part_title: KMS Authorization, Rotation and Multi-Region Keys

scenes.title: KMS access has three instruments
scenes.visual_overview: Three panels explain key policy, IAM permissions and grants, plus a two-account example.
visual_walkthrough: The key policy directly grants access or enables IAM policy delegation
IAM identity policy supplies permitted KMS actions where the key policy authorizes IAM use
Grants allow scoped operations for integrated services and other supported workflows
Cross-account example uses a customer managed key in Account A and a role in Account B
scenes.visual_example: A role in Account B requires appropriate IAM authorization in B and key policy permission in A for a cross-account KMS operation; grants may also participate in permitted designs.
scenes.visual_synthesis: A broad IAM Allow cannot override an absent or denying key policy; examine the entire KMS authorization path.
scenes.narration: This diagram separates three KMS authorization instruments. First, on the left, the key policy is the foundational policy attached to the KMS key. It can directly authorize a principal or allow IAM policies to control use of the key. Next, the middle panel shows an IAM identity policy on a user or role. For IAM policy permissions to apply, the key policy must provide the appropriate authorization or delegation. The right panel introduces grants, which give scoped cryptographic rights and are especially common with AWS services that use a key on behalf of workloads. Follow the bottom cross-account example. Account A owns a customer managed key, and a role in Account B wants to use it. The owner account must permit the external principal in the key policy, and the role in Account B must have suitable IAM permissions, with other relevant controls still applying. The slide's arrows illustrate authorization when both sides permit the operation. Don't assume an IAM AdministratorAccess policy alone is sufficient for KMS. Always check key policy, IAM permissions, applicable grants, resource ARN and policy conditions.

scenes.title: Rotation changes key material, not key identity
scenes.visual_overview: A customer managed symmetric KMS key retains its ID and policy while its cryptographic material changes, with old and new ciphertext still decryptable.
visual_walkthrough: Follow version-one key material to the rotation event
Observe version-two key material after rotation while the same KMS key ID and policy remain
Old ciphertext stays decryptable with historical key material
New encryptions use the current key material
scenes.visual_example: A KMS key used for existing encrypted objects rotates automatically when supported; existing objects do not need to be re-encrypted just because the backing key material rotated.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Differentiate key-material rotation from changing the KMS key ARN, re-encrypting existing data and rotating application secrets.
scenes.narration: This slide illustrates what really changes during AWS KMS key rotation. At the top is one customer managed symmetric KMS key with a stable key ID and key policy. The middle timeline shows version one of its cryptographic key material, a rotation event, and version two. The identity of the KMS key does not change when supported automatic or on-demand rotation replaces its underlying key material. Trace the lower left example. Data encrypted before rotation can still be decrypted using the historical backing material, managed by KMS. The lower right shows new encryption operations using the current backing material. That does not mean all existing data has been rewritten or re-encrypted during rotation. Automatic rotation eligibility depends on key type and origin; for imported material and some other key configurations, different procedures apply. The important decision is to distinguish changing backing key material from creating a replacement KMS key and from rotating database credentials. Each operation has different effects on encrypted data, permissions and recovery. Plan key ownership, deletion safety and application compatibility accordingly.

scenes.title: Multi-Region KMS keys: shared material, separate access
scenes.visual_overview: Primary and replica KMS keys in two AWS Regions have synchronized key ID and cryptographic material but separate ARNs, policies, aliases and grants.
visual_walkthrough: Left Region A contains the primary KMS key and its independent controls
Center depicts synchronized cryptographic key material and corresponding ciphertext
Right Region B contains a replica with its own IAM or key policy and grants
Cross-Region decrypt works only when replica permissions allow it
scenes.visual_example: Data encrypted using a multi-Region primary key in Region A may be decrypted using the matching replica in Region B when the caller is authorized and compatible cryptographic context is supplied.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Multi-Region keys support cryptographic interoperability but do not automatically replicate encrypted application data or IAM access policies.
scenes.narration: This diagram shows two AWS Regions with related KMS keys. Read the left panel first. Region A contains the primary multi-Region key and its own policy, grants, alias and ARN. The middle summary indicates that the matching replica shares the key ID and cryptographic material. Now inspect Region B on the right. Its key is a replica with separate Region-specific metadata, ARN, key policy and grants. The dashed synchronization arrow means the cryptographic material is coordinated; it does not mean every access-control decision is identical. Follow the ciphertext example along the bottom: data encrypted in Region A using the multi-Region key can be decrypted with the matching replica in Region B when the caller has appropriate permissions and the same required encryption context. That ability can support regional recovery and portable cryptographic operations. It does not copy an S3 bucket, database or other encrypted application data into the second Region, and it does not copy all policy permissions. Choose multi-Region keys when cross-Region cryptographic interoperability is a real requirement, then separately design data replication and regional authorization.
